ordered_diagnoses: Verrucous Carcinoma of the nasal vestibule

facts.raw_span: a mass in the right nostril that had been growing for about 1 year
The lesion bled with minimal trauma
did not obstruct his breathing
The patient did not smoke
denied any medical history of chronic rhinosinusitis
a 1-cm, nontender, exophytic, verrucous, skin-colored plaque on the right nasal vestibule
Papillary fronds with slender fibrovascular cores that are lined by nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium
Shows mucin-containing goblet cells
Neither cytologic atypia nor atypical mitotic figures are present
An exophytic, verrucous, and skin-colored plaque on the right nasal vestibule

concepts.why: The presence of papillary fronds with slender fibrovascular cores lined by nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium and mucin-containing goblet cells, without cytologic atypia or atypical mitotic figures, is consistent with inverted papilloma.

The exophytic and verrucous nature of the lesion, along with its tendency to bleed with minimal trauma, could suggest a malignant process such as squamous cell carcinoma, although the histologic findings do not support this diagnosis.
The verrucous appearance of the lesion and the presence of nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium could be consistent with verrucous carcinoma, a low-grade malignancy.
The presence of a mass in the nasal vestibule that does not obstruct breathing could be consistent with a nasal polyp, although the histologic findings do not support this diagnosis.

The presence of multiple papillary fronds with slender fibrovascular cores lined by nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium could be consistent with papillomatosis, a condition characterized by multiple inverted papillomas.
The presence of nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium without cytologic atypia or atypical mitotic figures could be consistent with squamous hyperplasia, a benign proliferative process.
The verrucous appearance of the lesion and the presence of nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium could be consistent with verrucous hyperplasia, a benign proliferative process.
The presence of a mass in the nasal vestibule with a tendency to bleed could suggest a malignant process such as nasal adenocarcinoma, although the histologic findings do not support this diagnosis.
